entry.title: Though I missed Callon, but met him anyway

link.title: Though I missed Callon, but met him anyway

entry.content:
<p>In the last post, I wrote about how I couldn’t make it to the tribute workshop for Michel Callon and instead had my own deep reading week. Now I’m trying to pull out what I learned from it, to ease the regret. Maybe it’s nice to start with how I got to know his name, which might not be so different from how others encountered him (if they did), but is still memorable and worth mentioning.</p><p>In South Korea, where I’m originally from, Callon is somewhat known as an ANT scholar who worked with Latour. In my experience, recognition mostly stops there, while Latour became a star intellectual, with many of his books and articles translated into Korean. ANT also became quite popular, but often got simplified into the proposition that “non-humans can also be actors,” more than anything else. I guess the “theory” in its name contributed to its gaining a foothold (maybe this is not only in Korea though).</p><p>The graduate school where I did my Master’s, STP (Science and Technology Policy), consisted of two cultures, namely policy studies and STS. I wasn’t really into STS at the moment, but that barely caused me any trouble under my advisor, a scholar of international comparative politics on the policy side. I also leaned toward policy, studying higher education policy and writing a thesis on university–industry cooperation to orient myself within so-called innovation studies. Still, the mandatory STS courses made me imagine crossing and linking these two cultures.</p>

<p>And somehow I found Callon, who seemed to be doing so, most notably by serving as an editor of Research Policy for 20 years, a journal I admired a lot. I should confess that I was really obsessed with the journal because of its name, its impact factor, and its (seeming) uniqueness. Even my initial interest in research misconduct, questionable research practices, and evaluation metric gaming might have come from its occasional publications on these topics. At least, finding them there reassured me that my interests were legitimate.</p><p>In addition, STP was somewhat divided between qualitative and quantitative methodologies along the same fault lines (a tendency sadly I also notice at CWTS and across science studies). I was again ambitious about integrating them and tried a bit (and will do so for my PhD). Finding that Callon was also a pioneer of co-word analysis, which opened up new directions for scientometrics and quantitative science studies, was inspiring to me in that sense.</p><p>However, by the time I left academia with my Master’s degree, that was it. I had perhaps read some of his classic pieces, but with only a superficial understanding or even just some impressions without much understanding at all.</p><h2 id="revisiting-callon">Revisiting Callon</h2><p>7 years had passed from then. When Callon passed away, I was busy wrapping things up in South Korea and preparing to move to the Netherlands for my PhD, having received the interview result from Wolfgang (my supervisor at CWTS) and accepted the offer after discussing it with my family. I might have heard the news through social media or somewhere else at the time, but I only really learned it later that year. That probably shows how little attention I was paying to him, or how little relevance I saw in his work for my research.</p><p>Then how did I really get into Callon? Looking back, I think there were two distinct but connected pathways through which I became a student of his work. I can't really tell which came first, so I tried to arrange them so they can be read in any order.</p><div class="kg-card kg-callout-card kg-callout-card-grey"><div class="kg-callout-text">Click each header to read more ↓</div></div><div class="kg-card kg-toggle-card" data-kg-toggle-state="close"> <div class="kg-toggle-heading"> <h4 class="kg-toggle-heading-text">Pathway from building a reading list</h4> </div> <div class="kg-toggle-content"><p>Starting my PhD, my aim for the first year was to read as much as I could and build my own bibliography (at least its core), which I could revisit throughout my PhD journey. That changed as time went by. I began to think of it more as navigating the landscape of academic publishing and understanding the context of my research topic: to avoid becoming too narrow, but also to know better where to draw the line and stop expanding (though I’m not really good at the latter). Now I’m trying to admit that I failed to read as much as I wanted (can anyone succeed at that these days?), but still built a good list of literature to refer to while doing empirical work. I justify this to myself by saying that reading never gets finished, so it’s better to blend it with doing research than to make it a precondition for my PhD.</p><p>Maybe the reason I shifted from reading to travelling (both literally and figuratively) was that I didn’t find the classics quite engaging enough, especially when reading them just to learn the disciplines. Still, the interview series in Engaging Science, Technology, and Society was an enjoyable read, much more so than much of the other literature, and led me to follow up on the references. Another helpful resource for studying STS was a recently published Encyclopedia of STS, which I also enjoyed, mostly because of its relatively short chapters focused on introducing themes. Soon I noticed two things: I hadn’t found an interview with Callon in the ESTS series, while his work (especially the scallop paper) seemed to appear as a core reading in almost every chapter of the encyclopedia.</p><p>No, I didn’t read the paper right away. Actually, I only read it just before writing this post, and I have mixed feelings about it. What I did then was search for an interview with him. I found one that was quite a gem, I’d say. Although it didn’t directly discuss his editorship, the conversation helped me understand how someone like Callon could have become and longly remained an editor of Research Policy.</p><p>He discussed how Mertonian sociology of science and mainstream economics of science shared assumptions about science while leaving its actual epistemic content and practices from empirical analyses and examinations. I should also note that Paula Stephan’s How Economics Shapes Science had been a go-to book during my Master’s. And I still see a close connection between the Mertonian tradition and scientometrics and quantitative science studies. His account put a finger on something that had been bothering me: why I had lost interest in these approaches while still sharing many of their research interests. (But I should also mention Callon has observed that Merton himself had recognized the limitations of this approach and was more receptive to studies of scientific practices than some of his followers.)</p><p>Reading this alongside the introductory chapters, I soon realized that it connected with my own struggles to understand why academia, at least in Korea, had changed so little after the surge of predatory publishing (which became known in Korean as “substandard scholarly/academic activities"). After engaging with these issues (I think I need another post for this though, speaking of my own 'sleuthing' experience), I had reached the point of questioning quantitative research assessment that outsourced its evaluative criteria to metrics and indicators. I had also started looking into valuation studies, which seemed to have something to say about what actually happens when people evaluate the epistemic quality of research.</p><p>I had only picked up this strand of thought at a surface level when applying for the PhD position. Now I was beginning to recognize connections between the vocabulary I had been using— from performativity, devices, arrangements and assemblages, to assetization—that they mostly came from, at least heavily rely on, the works of Callon, his collaborators, and scholars building on them. I had been using these terms without really understanding the conversations they originated. A shame but better late than never.</p></div> </div><div class="kg-card kg-toggle-card" data-kg-toggle-state="close"> <div class="kg-toggle-heading"> <h4 class="kg-toggle-heading-text">Pathway from observations around paper mills</h4> </div> <div class="kg-toggle-content"><p>I've spoken in public several times (even there's a video recording) about how I got interested in paper mills. The topic was given to me rather than formulated by myself, but I still chose to apply because it resonated with my own interests. One question I keep carrying is: to what extent are paper mills different from other research misconduct or questionable publishing practices? I had already seen predatory publishing up close, and I needed a reason to justify spending a whole PhD on this one, so some differentiation seemed necessary. My answer so far is that there is no single feature that is both necessary and sufficient to distinguish them.</p><p>Still, if I have to pick the feature that matters most to me, it's authorship-for-sale at scale. Selling authorship isn't new, but doing it as an organized business is what made a black market of academic publishing. It is a clear violation of publication ethics, and it's easy (and fair) to label paper mills as the bad guys. But it doesn't explain how their business became possible, nor what would make it stop working.</p><p>This is where Callon became useful to me, not as a theory to apply but as a way to ask a different question. Markets in the Making is a compendium of his thoughts on market studies, and a good part of it is about how markets are made and continuously remade: how goods are prepared to be traded, how participants are equipped to (e)valuate them, and how transactions become possible. Goods have to be detached from those who made them, framed to behave predictably, and attributed to someone entitled to transfer them.</p><p>Authorship appears among his examples too, when he contrasts how scientific discovery and invention are treated regarding property rights. His point is that this distinction made sense in the past but has become hard to sustain in technoscientific fields (p.98-101). Reading this, I thought paper mills push the same point from another direction. Authorship is supposed to stay attached to the person who did the work. But if who gets credited is a convention to begin with, it can be detached from the manuscript and made transferable for money. (And with AI-generated manuscripts, it's not even clear what there would be to attach to.) So they are not just breaking a rule, they are making a market.</p><p>Paper mills could do this only because the legitimate market had already made publication into a kind of currency. So we should ask: how does authorship become something that can be offered, priced, and transferred to a buyer? And what must happen for that purchased authorship to count within academic evaluation? We all share some responsibility here, yet while people recognize that collective action is necessary and take steps to combat paper mills, they are also busy blaming each other. More often than not, the blame lands on commercial actors, namely publishers. This brings me to another question I always keep in mind: why would publishers care about this at all? It may come from my positionality regarding the PhD project, but it is also something I've been asking even before then.</p><p>To be honest, I've become quite dissatisfied with "commercialization" being used as an explanation for what went wrong. It's a low hanging and easy argument to reach for, and yet powerful one in a society where so many things are being commercialized. The argument goes like: something we value seems to be deteriorating, commercial actors are involved, so commercialization must be the reason. I understand the appeal, and I used this narrative quite freely during my Master's. But toward the end of writing my thesis, I got tired of how often the conversation stopped there. From graduate students' rights to predatory publishing, the seniors who sympathized with my problems tended to direct them toward something so big and far away like neoliberalism that it felt useless for what we could actually investigate or change.</p><p>My dissatisfaction was not only that this seemed unhelpful for dealing with existing problems. I also doubted whether it was accurate, or at least precise enough. What exactly is changed through commercialization? By whom, through which arrangements, and with what consequences? These questions tend to disappear once commercialization has been named as the problem.</p><p>Then I found the term "marketization" in Callon's work. It doesn't necessarily moralize the market or commercialization. It tries to show how markets have been made and are constantly being made, and Callon insists on separating "market" from "capitalism," which the story that blames commercialization usually conflates. This is much more demanding, but it gives a more solid empirical ground for what is actually happening beyond "commercial actors ruin the subject." It also changes how I read ruining and extracting. What commercial actors leave out is not simply destroyed. It is what falls outside a particular framing, and for Callon it comes back as overflow, as concern and critique that feed the next round of market-making. Which makes me wonder whether commercial actors could also be allies, a question I'll come back to below.</p><p>Then, am I being uncritical about the commercialization of science? I should disclose more clearly that one of the biggest commercial publishers has made my PhD position possible, and it might have somewhat influenced the problematization above. But to be honest, it's more complicated than that. The first question, if not research question, I had since the start of my PhD was "why do publishers care about research integrity, and are they actually caring?" Partly because of where the research funding of mine comes from, but also because I see initiatives elsewhere in publishing where commercial actors are investing, though the amount and sincerity are arguable. Their existence is nevertheless something I want to understand.</p><p>I think criticism of academic publishers needs to go further than pointing out how much money they make from science. And I AM concerned about the race to commercialize research integrity, but not quite because it is commercial. To put it somewhat radically, I might not be bothered much about parts of scholarly communication being commercialized as such. What concerns me is the consequences: it changes the valuation regime in scholarly communication, which affects epistemology by influencing how science is done and disseminated. When an integrity intervention has to fit a commercial service or an existing business model, the solution space for the current problem is constrained to what is compatible with it, often beyond the researcher communities' control and sometimes heading in the opposite direction from what they want. But I'd like to treat this as an empirical question and follow up on how it comes to be so. Which problems receive attention? What can be recognized and acted upon through the tools being developed? Who decides what counts as a sufficient solution?</p><p>Nor do I think that invoking "publish or perish" or the current research assessment settles the explanation, though that doesn't mean they should go unblamed. How we got to the point where everyone says there is a crisis of peer review, research integrity, or trust in science (you name it) is not so hard to explain even without an economic model: scale has been benefiting both sides, so they just proceeded until now. I want to go further than saying researchers respond to incentives and publishers pursue revenue. What I'd like to understand is how the current situation is problematized by different actors with different interests, and how those interests become connected leading to some attempts toward solutions.</p><p>A small observation from this September shows what I mean here. Peer Review Week 2026 had the theme "Peer Review Capacity: Volume, Speed, and Quality," and organized by a steering committee of more than 50 industry organizations and societies. The theme, as the keywords show, was about how to scale peer review as a well-oiled system, and peer review here reads to me as a process of producing publication goods that is running short of capacity. And from what I saw, most events were hosted by and invited speakers from commercial actors, not by the "peers" who actually review. (But wait, you never know, vendor might recruit paid peer reviewers and they could have been there.)</p><p>This brings me back to the question from my reading notes, maybe the most radical one: can commercial actors become allies in changing these arrangements? There will surely be conflicts and frictions, and their interests will not always align with researchers. But I don't want to rule it out in advance. Reading Callon has made me more interested in what such cooperation would require, and what it could actually change.</p></div> </div><h2 id="so-now-what">So now what?</h2><p>Either way, I’ve quite enjoyed reading Callon’s work so far. He has left plenty to read, and there is even another book co-authored with Koray Çalışkan and Donald MacKenzie on the way coming early next year: Economization. Some of these works will definitely find a lasting place in my bibliography (and some will probably remain unread realistically, unless my PhD somehow becomes entirely about him).</p><p>What I’m picking up is his way of approaching markets and their infrastructures as always in the making—being designed, experimented with, fine-tuned, and (re)assembled. I’m also putting his language and vocabulary (or jargon)—passiva(c)tion, qualculation, framing, overflow—into my head, but trying not to make everything I observe into an example of a concept I’ve just learned. I still hesitate about following the broader scope of economization and ecologization which I didn't fully understand (and also read much about), so I’m not yet sure how far I need to follow it for my own research.</p><p>By doing so, I’d like to take further the popular metaphors about publications, especially their being a currency in academia, where research assessment relies heavily on journal publications and the culture of “publish or perish” becomes self-fulfilling. This longstanding folk theory fits the phenomenon of paper mills so well. Not to mention academic publishing itself, meanwhile, has long been a commercial business. Even well-intentioned open access initiatives have been taken up through business models based on APC (i.e. Gold OA), shifting payment from reading to publishing.</p><p>Our efforts to combat paper mills, now also flooded with all things AI, will contribute to making new market agencements, to borrow Callon’s term. Here, research integrity works as an imperative that brings together diverse actors around academic publishing. But how they frame it differs, and their responses have to fit established infrastructures and political economic arrangements, mostly those already in place. These responses also produce overflows, leaving further concerns to be contested through other experiments.</p><p>Publications, considered as goods within my current framework with reading Callon, may retain their formal conventions while their meaning keeps changing, as their markets are themselves always in the making. Scholarly communication will change along with them, though perhaps more slowly than we predict these days because of our sticky sociotechnical associations, alliances, assemblages, or agencements (I know they are not interchangeable, but now you get why I get tired of jargons). My PhD will trace this transformation without simply buying the narrative of a response to an external crisis of destruction, such as paper mills and AI, or of disruptive innovation from within, such as forensic techniques and, again, AI.</p><p>Indeed, it has been quite a satisfying time, full of inspiration from Michel Callon, and also from his co-authors and students. I now think I can go to Paris this winter with less regret and enjoy some sightseeing in peace.</p>
entry.summary: My week of reading Callon led me to make many connections with questions I had been thinking about regarding paper mills, and even broader academic publishing.

entry.title: My Dumbest Moment of 2026 (+ and my personal tribute to Michel Callon)

link.title: My Dumbest Moment of 2026 (+ and my personal tribute to Michel Callon)

entry.content:
<p>One thing I have become familiar with after spending months living in Europe is public transport delays (whether bus or train) and to complain about them. (Though I can already hear people from other European countries telling me how good I have it in NL ;)) After experiencing the worst of it in Italy, I tend to think nothing of it now. So usually, I'm not the problem when traveling, but this time I was so wrong that I can hardly believe what happened.</p><p>I recently learned about a tribute workshop for Michel Callon, who passed away last year, taking place last Tuesday at Mines Paris-PSL. It was dedicated to his contributions and furthering discussions on so-called 'market studies'. It was an one day in-person event, which had me calculating the time and money required for a trip to Paris. I finally decided to go, not because I felt I knew Callon well enough to jump into discussions with his well known friends and students. It was apposite, actually. I had an instinct that Callon’s work could provide a useful perspective and toolkit for my PhD research, however, I wasn't entirely sure how. I had always found his writing difficult and struggled to grasp how other scholars are engaging with him. So I figured the workshop would be a great overview of his contributions and a litmus test for whether I should dive deeper into his works.</p>

<p>I booked Eurostar ticket (Rotterdam <-> Paris) and a hostel for one night in a last-minute (a day trip was impossible). I booked an evening train for Monday so I could work as usual, come home for dinner, pack my bags, and depart by 8PM at the latest. No issues at all. Still, I rushed my bike ride to the station to catch the connecting train from Leiden to Rotterdam. I made it to the platform with plenty of time to spare.</p><p>Then, I checked my Eurostar ticket to see if it was delayed, only to realize that the Eurostar train's actual departure time was 8PM. So the train had already left Rotterdam, and I was still in Leiden. Since it was the last Eurostar of the day, there was no point in going to Rotterdam. I barely managed to hop off from my connecting train just before it departed. I stood there, spaced out for a moment, trying to process what had just happened.</p><p>Before giving in to regret, I checked if alternative transportation to Paris was possible. My only options were overnight buses or the next morning’s Eurostar, which would make me miss a third of the event. Both were quite expensive too. I was also already became tired with recent trips to Belgium for a summer school (ESSS) and a conference (STI-ENID). Attending an academic workshop that pretty sure to be difficult for me, in such a bad condition seemed like a terrible idea. Experiences have taught me that pushing myself rarely works out well. I gave up and went back home, appreciating that I had at least made the early decision not to head to Rotterdam.</p><p>I sat down to reflect on what happened, regretting not just the wasted money, but the missed opportunity to attend this monumental event in person. My brain had somehow mixed up "the train departs at 8PM" with "I should leave the house at 8PM." I thought I had added it to my calendar via the Eurostar app (spoiler: I actually did), but since it didn't show up on my immediate schedule, nothing corrected my false memory. What really struck me was how easily I could have realized my plan was impossible. I knew I was scheduled to arrive in Paris around 10:30PM, and the Eurostar takes about 2.5 hours, meaning it had to depart at 8PM from Rotterdam. A simple backward calculation could've prevented this, but I didn't.</p><p>Putting aside my FOMO, I decided to spend the whole day in Leiden hosting my own virtual tribute workshop on Michel Callon. I read excerpts from his book Markets in the Making (2021) alongside reviews, notably a three part series of essays published in the Journal of Cultural Economy last year. I had only hinted at the relevance of Callon's market studies to my conceptual framework and methodology in my research proposal. But by taking this opportunity (not sure whether it has worked better than attending the actual workshop) to have some concentrating time solely on his writings and the reviews, I gained clarity on what I can extract from this strand of research meaningfully. I will write about that in a separate piece, as this post is already longer than expected.</p><p>Later that same week, my wife had the opportunity to attend a K-pop group's world tour concert in Paris through an acquaintance. While helping her find a suitable train ticket, I opened the Eurostar app and was shocked to see that the ticket I thought I had missed was still there. I soon discovered that I had actually booked a ticket for Dec 14, not Sep 14. It's likely that I mixed them up because both dates fall on Monday.</p><p>This explained why the schedule only appeared in my December calendar and not on my September page. This also meant that even if I hadn't confused the time and made it to Rotterdam before 8PM, I wouldn't have been able to board the train anyway. (Lucky me?) So, I didn't completely blow my ticket, though I'm not sure if it makes sense to go to Paris for two random days in December without an event to attend.</p><p>I promised my wife I would publicly reflect on this so it never happens again. By posting this, I hope to turn this experience into a lasting lesson. To avoid being this dumb again: I must double-check the exact date and time on my tickets (hopefully before hitting the "purchase" button…), ensure they sync properly to my calendar, and verify everything twice.</p><p>My apologies to Michel Callon (and to the organizers at Mines Paris-PSL for the no-show registration). I couldn't be there in person for your tribute, but rest in peace. I will be sure to continue your endeavor of studying markets and contribute in my own way.</p>
entry.summary: I was supposed to be in Paris this Tuesday, but ended up just reading his book in Leiden.

entry.title: Can We Really Just “Keep Calm and Carry On”? (STS NL 2026)

link.title: Can We Really Just “Keep Calm and Carry On”? (STS NL 2026)

entry.content:
<p>I feel really bad that I'm writing this so late, even more than a month passed after STS-NL conference. This is partly because I was caught up in my own work (which ironically relates to the experience I'm going to write about), but also because I usually like to let my thoughts brew over time rather than responding immediately. Both approaches have pros and cons, but I'll try to share my thoughts more quickly now that I have this new personal venue for writing.</p><p>At STS-NL, a very familiar type of incident happened, but it ended in an unusual way.</p><p>There was a technical issue during the WTMC 40th anniversary plenary, an electrical noise suddenly burst and filled the whole lecture hall. So far, so usual… We experience these things quite often, and I bet everyone expected it to be resolved quickly.</p>

<p>But the thing was, it didn't. It felt like it went on for dozens of minutes (though it might be probably shorter in reality). Assistants tried to fix it, but eventually, they all failed, and Sally Wyatt, acting as chair, had to wrap the session up early. It was barely possible to hear her voice over the noise, but we understood what we had to do through her gestures.</p><p>Because the plenary took place in a separate building to accommodate the large audience, we had to exit and walk back to the main venue. The doors even required an officer to scan a card for every person leaving, so it took quite a while to finally escape the sound.</p><p>For me, this felt like a metaphor for the current status of STS, or even academia at large.</p><p>Earlier in that same session, before the noise started, there was a Q&A between the audience and the panel. One of early career researchers asking Wiebe Bijker what we should do as STSers in these troubled times, with extremists distracting and misleading the public as the world gets worse. I honestly cannot remember fully the whole question or the exact context, but it reminded me of ongoing wars, the climate crisis, or even the AI hype-driven tech-oligarchy.</p><p>Surprisingly, Wiebe Bijker answered by quoting the famous UK slogan, "Keep Calm and Carry On." This left people feeling somewhat unsatisfied, and I guess it even grated on some nerves. Later, he mentioned he might have picked the wrong phrase and clarified that he meant we shouldn't get dragged down by the rhetoric, but rather focus on what we can do and what we do best: rigorous and robust research.</p><p>I don't want to refute his answer, and I do somewhat agree with him. To be honest, I am a person who feels more comfortable being a researcher who sits in an office chair, observes things, writes down my thoughts, and derives scholarly ideas from them.</p><p>But as someone who always feels a sense of indebtedness to activists, his answer was not resonating this time. Maybe I wanted—even if they were just words—some encouragement to act against it, to raise our voices, and to find more ways for direct political responses, not just as citizens, but as researchers allying with the citizens.</p><p>It was not directly after that conversation (and if it was, it would have felt like a divine(?) sign to us all..!), but not long after, the sound incident happened.</p><p>The metaphor that struck me was this: there is definitively a sound, an event, or an environment that makes all of us stop doing our work.</p><p>When we can no longer do what we are used to doing under certain circumstances, we have to hastily disperse. And I ask: what if now is that time? What if everything we see and feel—which genuinely looks like a crisis—is the noise that happened in that hall? What if this is a case where we cannot just "keep calm and carry on"? Then what should we do? What are our responsibilities as STSers, researchers, and academics?</p><p>Coincidentally, though, there was a WTMC workshop a month later, and the reading list included an old article asking what STS is for, and how it is forgetting its connection to activists' critical thoughts and practices (Martin, 1993). I enjoyed reading it while recalling this anecdote.</p><p>This struck me so hard that I actually consider this experience more important than my first presentation as a PhD at the conference. I was indeed thinking about what kind of research I wanna do, and who I wanna be as a researcher when I decided to shift my career from industry back to academia. Of course, I don't have an answer right now, and I won't try to force one here. I even think I can think of an answer in near future. Paradoxically I'll just carry on with this afterthought myself, but I'm not sure if I could keep calm enough when doing so.</p><h3 id="reference">Reference</h3><p>Martin, B. (1993). The Critique of Science Becomes Academic. Science, Technology, & Human Values, 18(2), 247–259. https://doi.org/10.1177/016224399301800208</p>
entry.summary: When the noise of the world gets too loud, can researchers really just "keep calm and carry on"? Thoughts from STS-NL on academic responsibility, personal reflection on my uncomfortable preference sitting on the quiet office chair, and finding my path as an early-stage PhD.

entry.title: Trapped in the Iron Cage: The One-Dimensional Researcher

link.title: Trapped in the Iron Cage: The One-Dimensional Researcher

entry.content:
✍️
I originally wrote this piece back in 2019 for Behind Sciences in Korean, a magazine run by graduate students at the university where I did my Master's. When I was applying for the PhD in 2025--so 6 years gap there, I had to submit 3 writing samples but didn't have enough pieces in English. I decided to translate this one because it clearly illustrates the background and context of how I first became interested in the systemic problems related to academic publishing. While I'm not sure how much this contributed to get through the review, I assume it didn't work badly, given that I started my PhD! I'm sharing it here as the inaugural post on this blog for the record.

You can also find the original Korean version of this article at: https://behindsciences.kaist.ac.kr/2019/12/23/

“12 points, 8, 15 but as a second author, so roughly 10 points. Wow, he published here? Another 10 points. What’s this one? Don’t know, pass. Oh yeah, people are definitely getting publishing here a lot. 3, 3, 7, ..."2

During my undergraduate years majoring in Materials Science and Engineering, I wasn't certain about pursuing graduate school, so I decided to gain some research experience first. My academic advisor introduced me to a senior student in his lab, suggesting I come by and learn about experiments. However, on my very first day, what the senior taught me wasn't experimental techniques, but rather how to read a researcher's CV (curriculum vitae). We were in the middle of discussing which lab I might consider for my graduate program. He scanned the publication list of a newly appointed professor in the department and began calculating points as if grading an exam paper. After repeating this a few times with different professors’ lists, he recommended a “good” one to me. Although bewildered at first, I found it quite impressive, thinking, “So this must be how researchers evaluate and recognize one another. Cool!”.

It wasn’t until around the time I finished my undergraduate degree that I realized the numbers the senior student had been reciting were Journal Impact Factors3. Whenever I spoke with friends who had already started graduate school, the conversation invariably touched upon publishing papers, and the Impact Factor was always a central theme. Even on social media, it wasn’t uncommon to see posts boasting about where someone had published a paper, followed by numerous congratulatory comments. Interestingly, the actual content and process of the research itself rarely became the main topic of conversation.

I ended up in graduate school too, even though I changed my major to social sciences. Had my seniors emphasized it that much, or did I just take it too seriously? Before I could even finish my first semester, thoughts of “I need to publish papers quickly” began filling my mind. And so, as a new master’s student who hadn’t even determined my own research topic yet, I lived by the maxim “Publish or Perish.” Before long, I found myself considering what and how to research in order to publish numerous papers in high impact factor journals as quickly as possible.

My strategy was reasonable enough. I examined which journals had published the papers listed in my advisor’s course syllabus. I selected the journals with the highest impact factors, investigated what kind of research topics had been published in recent years, and how frequently those papers were cited. After becoming familiar with academic search engines like Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, and after skimming through hundreds of abstracts without reading most of the actual papers, it became abundantly clear that I needed to research academia-industry collaboration. And that’s how I determined my research topic.

Now I found myself drawn to the internet communities like hibrain.net (Korean website for academic job network), where university faculty job vacancies are posted. These sites shared information about how many publication points a PhD researcher needs to meet requirements for a new faculty position, and how many points count for papers published in KCI (Korea Citation Index) and SCI indexed journals4. There were plenty of “insider tips” too, like how combining several published papers into a book would count both the papers and the book as separate achievements, but writing a book first would prevent you from publishing the same content as papers, so it was better to delay writing a book. While I was preoccupied with figuring out survival strategies in academia, I heard news that my graduate school was hiring a new professor. As soon as I learned the names of the finalists, I found myself, just like that senior student from my undergraduate days, scrutinizing the number of publications from each candidate, where they were published, whether the journals were indexed in SCI, and their impact factors. Of course, I never actually read the papers.

Accelerated academy and publication as academic currency

I imagine academia filled with like-minded individuals. Every researcher evaluates others based solely on their CVs with a long list of publications and impact factors of the journals where they have published. Researchers desperately try to publish as many papers as possible in journals that are indexed in SCI or Scopus with higher impact factors. Research institutions pursue the same goals. Academic societies likewise do everything they can to get their journals included in indexing databases and to increase their impact factors. And so academia marches relentlessly toward more papers, more indexed journals, and higher impact factors5.

This isn’t merely a hypothetical scenario. Ugo Bardi, an Italian physical chemist, has pointed out that the “publish-or-perish” atmosphere, combined with a permissive peer review system that functions as a lax gatekeeper, is pushing academia toward mass production of papers. He argues that this situation, where researchers are forced to write too many papers, paradoxically demonstrates the decline of scholarship6. According to Bardi, scientific papers in today’s research system share similar characteristics with currency in the modern economy (see Table 1). Furthermore, he draws a stark comparison: academia’s fixation on paper quantity is as fundamentally unsustainable as economic systems that deplete natural resources in pursuit of endless consumption and profit maximization.

Table 1: What Currency and Papers Have in Common7

Emitting currency. Just as central banks issue currency, papers are only given value through the citation indexing services.
Spending your currency. A paper has no value in itself. It is only exchangeable like currency when you get a research grant or a job.
Inflation. Currency and papers gradually lose value. Older papers are less valuable, so individual researchers have to keep writing new papers.
Interest on currency. Just as money in the bank earns interest, researchers submit a list of their publications to funding organizations to receive funding and generate more research output.
Assaying. Just as coins and banknotes are issued after being verified by an authorized organization, papers are also verified through a process called peer review before being distributed.
Counterfeiting. Bad journals are published without verification, just like counterfeit bills.
Bad money replaces the good. Just as bad money drives out good money in economics (Gresham’s Law), papers are often valued by their quantity rather than quality, resulting in a proliferation of low-quality publications.
Ponzi schemes and multi-level marketing. A business model that travels across time and place is also strategically utilized by many bogus journals.


Academia isn’t solely focused on maximizing paper counts. Extending Ugo Bardi’s idea, we can interpret that papers have different “exchange rates” based on the journals they appear in and those journals’ impact factors. Depending on how frequently a paper is cited, it might experience a slower rate of “inflation” or even undergo “deflation” in some cases. Other types of academic “currency” also exist, such as patents, technology transfers, and research grants. All these currency values combine to determine the worth of individual researchers, and further extend to ranking universities or research institutes, and even entire countries. It’s similar to how companies are ranked by revenue or market value, and nations by GDP or economic growth rates.

There’s no upper limit to the performance metrics that determine a researcher’s worth, but research funding and job opportunities are finite, even scarce. Competition is therefore inevitable. Within academia’s race to maximize performance indicators, there are researchers who simultaneously pursue multiple research projects to maintain a continuous stream of publications. They experience an acceleration not just in the growing number of papers, but in every aspect of academic life. A research group led by Czech theoretical sociologist Filip Vostal has termed this phenomenon the “Accelerated Academy” and organizes academic seminars under the same name8. This acceleration refers not only to the increased rate at which researchers publish, but also to the intensified time pressure they experience. Real-world researchers cannot devote themselves exclusively to conducting research as their time is limited. Meanwhile, performance standards continually rise on all fronts: for continuing research, gaining recognition in one’s field, and achieving personal satisfaction. As a result, time becomes an ever more precious commodity.

Paradoxically, it’s the early-career researchers who both drive academia’s acceleration and become its casualties. Unlike their senior colleagues who have already established their positions, these newcomers frequently find themselves eliminated from the race despite publishing significant numbers of papers. As a result, endless pressure, anxiety, and stress are their daily reality. Indeed, recent studies have consistently revealed serious mental health concerns among doctoral students and early-career researchers9.

In response to these desperate pleas, some emphasize the need for advising from supervisors and senior researchers, as well as systematic mental health services11. But can these measures do more than merely alleviate the immediate symptoms? I once found myself confiding in my advisor when I couldn’t bear the stress and anxiety anymore. In the back of my mind, I was also frustrated with our department’s curriculum, which focused more on critical reading seminars than on paper writing. While I complained, my professor listened quietly before dismissing me with a single sentence: “Good researchers eventually find good positions anyway.” That was something she could say because she was already a professor. But it was also perhaps the best thing she could say in her position.

The classes I took in other departments, almost as if escaping, were uniformly practical. They covered everything: choosing research topics, examining relevant journals, finding resources for the latest research methodologies, understanding journal editors’ preferences, and writing papers. Every aspect of these courses was aligned with efficient paper publication strategies. Just attending these classes brought me a sense of relief.

One professor scheduled time with students individually during the midterm period to read and provide feedback on their research proposals. I was grateful that this professor, who had consistently published in so-called “top journals,” showed such dedication even to students from other departments. At the time, I was deeply interested in university entrepreneurship policies and told the professor I wanted to conduct case analyses and interviews to develop a theory explaining necessity-driven entrepreneurship, a topic rarely addressed in previous studies. The professor immediately waved dismissively and said, “No, no. That kind of research is for established scholars. It would be difficult to publish in top journals with that approach.” It struck me then: while I had strategically chosen my research field, why had I overlooked the fact that research content including topics and methodologies also needed to be selected strategically?

Peer review and Researcher Identity Constructed by Performance Metrics

In fact, academia has always functioned as both a financial system and a competitive society. What makes the discussions by Bardi, Vostal, and the “Accelerated Academy” research group novel is their focus on how academia’s operation as them has changed by time. Traditionally, the currency circulating in academia was recognition. Researchers were concerned more with authorship than with paper counts. Beyond copyright issues, plagiarism was considered a violation of research ethics precisely because it attempted to steal recognition from others. Researchers accumulated recognition to build reputation, secure positions, and obtain research funding.

Academia recognizes only firsts. The famous dispute between Newton and Leibniz over who first developed calculus is a well-known example. This explains why many researchers still worry about being “scooped”12, having their ongoing research published by someone else first. In a world that only remembers the first, fierce competition is inevitable. Academia has always been a competitive society where recognition is the prize.

Recognition stems from interaction. To recognize someone, you must either directly understand their research or at least make your own judgment based on evaluations from others in the same field. Einstein is praised as a great scientist not simply because of his 300 publications in prestigious journals and citations; rather, it was the acknowledgement of other scientists who actually read and evaluated his work. In a research system based on recognition, researchers’ self-identities were formed within a network where peers continuously assessed and acknowledged each other’s work.

Today, however, researchers’ self-identities are constructed by performance metrics. Their CVs display endless lists of publications rather than a description or the significance of the research done. Simultaneously, genuine peer review culture is vanishing from academia. There’s no need to spare precious time to scrutinize what other researchers are studying, whether their methods are robust or results are valid, and if there are any implications. Just after two or more anonymous reviewers approve, we consider it deserves publication. Papers in journals indexed in citation databases like SCI seem even more trustworthy. Researchers have effectively outsourced their role of evaluation, with citation indexing services and performance metrics filling the void. Without these, academia as we know it could no longer function because the research system has transformed into a financial system and competitive society where higher performance indicators replace genuine recognition13.

Performance metrics have established themselves as the new operating principles of academia through two main legitimation mechanisms. First, they allegedly allowed for productive and efficient management of research activities at various scales. Second, compared to recognition-based evaluation with its unclear criteria and foundations, metrics were perceived as rational and objective, thus becoming the standard measure for evaluating both researchers and their work.

However, as already pointed out, the first mechanism has actually made academia unsustainable rather than improving it. It’s also well documented that the supposed increases in productivity and efficiency resulting from the management of metrics are merely an illusion14.

The second mechanism also deserves careful scrutiny regarding what rationality and objectivity truly mean in research evaluation. American sociologist Michèle Lamont’s observations of peer review sessions revealed not a simple measurement of academic excellence, but rather a complex deliberative process15. In these settings, researchers exchanged viewpoints across various criteria - originality, methodology, feasibility - and continuously negotiated both the meaning and relative importance of each criterion. Subjects to be evaluated were often interpreted differently, sometimes leading to clashes between individual or disciplinary values. In short, evaluation results emerged only after a complex process of deliberation and consensus-building.

Performance metrics, however, lack this deliberative process. There’s insufficient consideration of what characteristics these metrics possess, what values they incorporate or exclude. Lamont questions whether performance indicators can truly be rational and objective, or to put it differently, whether rationality and objectivity should be the primary values when determining research evaluation methods. This leads us to reflect on what advantages performance metrics offer over researchers who strive for rational and objective evaluations, despite recognizing their own limitations? Are we perhaps mistaking metrics for rationality and objectivity simply because they are quantitative?

Escaping from Being the One-dimensional Researcher in the Iron Cage

After a year of persistent investigative reporting by Newstapa, the issue of fraudulent academic activities became a major controversy both within and outside academia16. Meaningless sham conferences where anyone could take the podium and say anything as long as they paid a registration fee; predatory journals that would publish virtually any article regardless of quality if publication fees were paid; and researchers who used research funds for these activities and then submitted the resulting publications as legitimate achievements - all provoked significant public outrage. Korean government identified and disciplined researchers who had attended the conferences mentioned in the reports17. The impact was so significant that even a nominee for Minister of Science, Technology, and ICT was forced to withdraw due to controversy over his attendance at a predatory conference.

The report from a survey conducted by the Biological Research Information Center (BRIC) after the incident reveals how the academic community perceives questionable research practices18. Researchers identified "quantitative research evaluation metrics" (34%) and "individual researchers' academic dishonesty" (33%) as the primary causes of the issue. Only 14%, which is less than half of either of the top responses, pointed to "internal apathy, indifference, and loss of healthy oversight within academia." Regarding institutions that should take responsibility, "research funding organizations" and "government departments" were the most frequently mentioned (34% and 24%, respectively). In contrast, only 8% believed that individual academic societies, which constitute the fundamental units of the academic community, should be held accountable. Researchers' perceptions influenced reporting by various media outlets, including Newstapa19, and ultimately were deeply reflected in the policy reforms announced by the government in May of this year to conclude the overall responses to the situation20. The approach framed questionable research practice as a problem, identified quantitative research evaluation and lack of research ethics as its causes, and established a causal relationship between them.

According to the causal relationship defined by researchers and the government, questionable research practices would disappear if quantitative evaluation were converted to qualitative evaluation and researchers received ethics training. However, the scope of questionable research practices is too ambiguous to hastily define it as a problem. Even Jeffrey Beall, the professional librarian who greatly contributed to raising awareness about questionable academic publishing, labeled his blacklist as “Potentially, possibly, or probably predatory publishers.” The proposed solutions seem equally hollow. What does qualitative evaluation actually entail? Does limiting the number of papers that can be listed in achievement sections to five while including citation counts and journal impact factors to constitute qualitative assessment? Similarly, research ethics awareness cannot be effectively raised by merely adding new clauses to the list of research misconduct only after media brings attention to them.

I interpret the emergence of questionable research practices, the establishment of quantitative research evaluation as a concrete system, and the lack of research ethics awareness among researchers as phenomena all stemming from the same cause. It is the reality that performance indicators constituting researchers’ self-identity, and these researchers in turn constituting an academia of, by, and for performance indicators. Rather than hastily proposing solutions, I hope researchers and the government will quickly recognize this uncomfortable truth, and diagnose and examine the current state of academia at first.

As a researcher, I left graduate school without significant accomplishments, fearing endless anxiety and pressure about maintaining a livelihood. I attributed the fears that constantly overwhelmed me to my lack of perseverance and talent. However, looking back from outside the university, I realized what I truly feared wasn’t making a living. Rather, I was afraid of becoming a one-dimensional researcher who only maximizes performance metrics within a cage-like academia where everything is legitimized by indicators. I want to find my identity as a researcher through endless interactions with other researchers. I hope my work contributes to the academic community I build together with other scholars, rather than just lengthening my CV or securing another research grant. In this way, I hope academia develops more slowly but more solidly.
